I don’t have a way to probe your network from here, so I can’t tell you your current download/upload speeds directly.  
But you can quickly find out yourself with a few simple steps:

---

## 1. Use an online speed‑test website

The easiest way is to visit one of the popular speed‑test sites:

| Site | URL |
|------|-----|
| Speedtest by Ookla | https://www.speedtest.net |
| Fast.com (Netflix) | https://fast.com |
| Xfinity Speed Test | https://speed.xfinity.com |
| Google “speed test” (Google’s own test) | Just type “speed test” into Google and click the “Run Speed Test” button |

Open the site in your browser, click the “Go” or “Start” button, and it will measure:

* **Download speed** (how fast data comes to you)
* **Upload speed** (how fast data goes from you)
* **Ping / latency** (how quickly your computer can talk to the server)

---

## 2. Run a command‑line test (if you prefer terminal)

If you’re comfortable with the command line, you can use the free `speedtest-cli` tool.  
It works on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

### a. Install `speedtest-cli`

#### Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
pip install speedtest-cli
```

> *If you don’t have Python or pip installed, you can download the installer from https://www.python.org/downloads/.*

#### macOS / Linux

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install speedtest-cli

# Linux (apt for Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install speedtest-cli
```

### b. Run the test

```bash
speedtest
```

or, if you want a concise output:

```bash
speedtest --simple
```

This will print something like:

```
Ping: 12.34 ms
Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
```

---

## 3. Check your router or modem

Many modern routers have a built‑in speed‑test page:

1. Log into your router’s admin interface (usually `http://192.168.0.1` or `http://192.168.1.1`).
2. Look for a “Status”, “Diagnostics”, or “Speed Test” section.
3. Run the test directly from the router.

---

## 4. Contact your ISP

If the measured speeds are consistently lower than what you’re paying for, you may want to:

1. Verify the plan details (e.g., “up to 100 Mbps”).
2. Ask the ISP to run a line test from their end.
3. Check for outages or maintenance in your area.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| Online website | No setup, works in any browser | Requires a web connection |
| `speedtest-cli` | Works from terminal, scriptable | Needs Python/pip |
| Router diagnostics | Directly measures line | Depends on router firmware |
| ISP support | Professional assistance | May take time |

Pick whichever method feels most convenient for you. If you run into any trouble setting up `speedtest-cli` or interpreting the results, let me know and I’ll walk you through it!
